uncertainties: Dione in verse 17 is provisionally identified with the Oceanid Dione in verse 353. The local source gives no explicit distinction, but does not expressly equate them.
Typhaon and Typhoeus are treated as forms of Typhon, following the supplied cards' identification; the Greek uses different name forms.
The Fates have two parentages in this source: Night in verses 217–218 and Themis with Zeus in verses 901–905. Their shared identities do not choose between these accounts.
Ker and the plural Keres receive separate individual and collective entries. The relationship between the Keres and the named Fates in verses 217–222 is not completely clear.
Echidna's parentage and the mothers indicated by pronouns in the monster genealogy can be disputed. No shared identity description resolves those pronouns beyond what is necessary.
The first woman is unnamed in this poem. Pandora is retained only as the identification supplied by the cards, without importing another poem's story.
Chrysaor, Medea, Phaethon, and Aristaeus are not assigned a uniform, fixed human or divine status beyond what the local source supports.

The two Doris bindings in p020 retain their original separate card and verse scopes: the Oceanid mother belongs to verse 241, and the Nereid daughter to verse 250. Their shared name must remain scope-sensitive.

The Cythera/Cytherea and Cyprus/Cyprus-born cards mix geography with Aphrodite's titles. Only Cytherea and Cyprus-born bind to Aphrodite; the island names and combined labels remain part of the unchanged contextual cards.
The river Triton in verse 929m remains a local geographical explanation. It is not bound to Triton the sea god, and its uncertain location is not resolved.
Permessus and Olmeius remain geographical river explanations because these lines do not identify them as divine persons. The genealogical Rivers and their named sons are registered as gods.
Philyra and Aeson are proved locally through family-name forms, Φιλυρίδης and Αἰσονίδης, rather than standalone personal names.
Grouped cards retain one shared contextual explanation, while their component figure names bind separately. Whole phrases naming different figures are not aliases of any one figure.
